newsitem.title: USA: Simpson depicts ex-wife as erratic, troubled woman.
newsitem.headline: Simpson depicts ex-wife as erratic, troubled woman.

text.p: Returning to the witness stand, O.J. Simpson on Friday depicted his ex-wife as a troubled woman who pursued him after their divorce, confided in him about becoming pregnant by another man and had wild mood swings.

The former football star, who was subjected to three days of bruising interrogation by opposing lawyers earlier in his civil trial, faced gentler questioning this time from his own lead defence attorney, Robert Baker.

Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 in the murders of his ex-wife and her friend, was one of the last defence witnesses scheduled to testify in the wrongful-death civil case brought by the victims' families.

Soon after Simpson took the stand, it became clear that Baker was determined to counter the plaintiffs' picture of a jealous, raging killer by portraying him instead as a concerned friend and confidant to Nicole Brown Simpson. He was expected to conclude his testimony on Monday.
Looking calm and composed, his baritone voice resounding through the crowded courtroom, Simpson expressed frustration about his ex-wife's sometimes erratic behavor.
At one point only a few months before the June 1994 murders, Simpson said he called her mother and said, "Something is going on and I'm concerned about it."
"One day it would be the Nicole you knew and the next day the Nicole you didn't. Did that continue?" Baker asked.
"Yes," Simpson said.

In testimony that could further sully his ex-wife's image to the jury, Simpson told of how she had called him in 1992 after their breakup and confided that she had become pregnant by another man. In opening arguments last October, Baker told jurors Nicole Brown Simpson aborted the pregnancy.
Also in 1992, Simpson said that one day when he went to Nicole Brown Simpson's apartment, he glanced through the window and saw her performing oral sex on her boyfriend.
"Did you get in a rage?" Baker asked.
"No, I was stunned," Simpson replied. He said he walked away but later asked them to be "a little more discreet with the kids around."
Simpson testified that it was his ex-wife who pursued him after their divorce seeking a reconciliation and not the other way around, as the plaintiffs had contended.
Baker had previewed his strategy of attacking Nicole Brown Simpson's character during opening arguments, portraying her as a promiscuous woman who abused drugs and ran with an unsavory crowd.
Some legal experts said Baker would have to tread carefully or else run the danger of alienating the jury.
"When you attack somebody who's been killed in this fashion, you run a high risk," said defence attorney Luke McKissack, a prominent Los Angeles legal analyst.
During Friday's testimony, Baker gave Simpson a chance to give his side of the story in response to allegations of domestic violence.

Simpson acknowledged that he was "very physical" with Nicole Brown Simpson in the early hours of New Year's Day 1989 in an incident that ultimately led to Simpson pleading no-contest to spousal abuse.
But he testified: "I didn't hit her. I didn't slap her. My intention was was not to hurt her in any way at all. ... I was told she fell outside my house (after the argument)."

Attorneys for the victims' families contend that Simpson beat, terrorised and finally murdered his ex-wife when he could no longer control her. They showed jurors photos of her bruised, swollen face, and called witnesses who described incidents of domestic violence.
With the trial nearing an end, analysts said Simpson's appearance was certain to be a major deciding factor in whether he wins or loses the case.
The case is expected to go to the jury before the end of January, after just three months of testimony -- a far cry from the nine months it took in Simpson's criminal trial.
If at least nine of the 12 jurors find him responsible for the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, Simpson could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages.
